items.title: The mighty return of the handmade.
items.subtitle: A handmade brand world; luxury brands have a verdict. And everyone agrees.
items.excerpt: Today’s post will make an attempt at understanding a cultural shift that has been happening in front of our eyes. A phenomenon in the making. This is a forecast report to understand the value and meaning behind using handmade content in brand worlds. But of course, told by me.…
items.html:
Today’s post will make an attempt at understanding a cultural shift that has been happening in front of our eyes. A phenomenon in the making. This is a forecast report to understand the value and meaning behind using handmade content in brand worlds. But of course, told by me. And I like a little storytelling.

Sketches, oil paintings, paper mache, riso print, analogue photography and other thousands of mediums an artist can embark on practicing and experimenting with; are obviously not new. Their existence is permanent in the human concourse. Because essentially, physical expression is invented by the body itself. Meaning the processes, even an analogue camera, are invented for the human body. Point and shoot. Then develop using chemicals, where a physical change followed by a chemical process results in photo capturing. Sketches are literally mark making. Oil paint, invented centuries ago, is oil and colour pigments. These mediums make sense to us, in the most primal way. Because of the transparency of their working principles. Cutting something, pasting it using glue. Which is why we sense how difficult it is to achieve the beauty of art we see. And we value the craft, in the form of dollars and praises.

Subscribe now

The hard launch of generative AI has triggered a cultural shift. Among others, it has changed the way we evaluate human made things. The word handmade was never an insult. It only added extra value way before AI. The word handmade implies something is slower and more costly than a mass produced alternative. Hands on. Deprived of rapidness, something that takes time. Made based on skill and craft. It is the complete opposite of what AI premise is. AI is practical, because you only need cents and a tap on a button for it to function. You don’t need a photographer, an art director, a model, and more. But with it comes ambiguity and opaqueness. Middle steps and process completely invisible. Tiny decisions detached from the grasp of the maker. Less control compared to what analogue and handmade presents. The originality of the outcome is a whole other argument which I will not dive into.

“The hard launch of generative AI has triggered a cultural shift. Among others, it has changed the way we evaluate human made things.”

Brands build their worlds to become immersive identities. These identities are then bought into by the customers. But more than that, it means immortality. A brand defying death means it has successfully become relatable with the current time but kept itself consistent enough to establish trust and persuasiveness. Substack is a rich place to write about brands and their worlds. I am particularly interested in the shifts in visual choices.

Scanned art and handmade mediums have been used in branding and world building quite frequently, way before generative AI ghosted our creative lives. Some design concepts just can’t function without a physical touch. It brings meaning and layers of storytelling. It is a design choice. Part of the craft. But the use of it after generative AI is intentional. Because there has to be a reason to choose the option where you just have to walk that extra mile and spend the extra dollar. The choice carries a bigger meaning.

Leave a comment

Hermes is one of the biggest examples because the whole brand narrative is constructed on it being far from reach. There is a real barrier with the customer who would like to acquire the most sought after Hermes products, not even taking the price tag into account. Yet it is Hermes who collaborates with real artists each season, and even goes to the extent to where the website is transformed into a fully hand sketched interface. The tactile world making conveys the idea that it was for sure made by a human. It was, for sure, a human brain who decided on the smallest gestures on the drawing. The artwork’s inspirations are undetectable. A naiveness and sense of play is on display. Because it’s the human brain who did it. The amount of tiny references artists make in their pieces, the smallest snaps of electricity are impossible to be faked. Real magic. Real creativity. Which establishes an unspoken trust of craft between the customer and the brand. Which then, is rendered as a valuable brand to relate to.

Paper based set designs have also become phenomena themselves. The play between 2D with 3D has mesmerized us. I cannot count how many times I have seen a Tiktok where the designer first prints out the design, then scans it again for the grainy look. However, mind you, I think this is far from an anti-ai movement. It is a natural sympathy towards what looks tactile and touchable. Might as well call it pro-physical. Perhaps we can trace this sympathy all the way to the first wave of offline It Girls everyone adored becoming. We would never drop our digital lives, but it was a refreshing fantasy to see the offline embodied. Offline made sense, because it was a reenactment of dropping the online mask everyone creates. It was seductive. Because it was so hard to acquire. Real people making things will gradually become harder and harder to acquire; with the economy in the state it is in today and AI getting cheaper and more capable each day.

“Might as well call it pro-physical. Perhaps we can trace this sympathy all the way to the first wave of offline It Girls everyone adored becoming. We would never drop our digital lives, but it was a refreshing fantasy to see the offline embodied. Offline made sense…It was seductive. Because it was so hard to acquire.”

Regardless of the technological developments in the scene, we will be demanding real and physical looking brand worlds. The brands who show the backstage, the raw footages will succeed in building believable and physical brand worlds. They will embrace transparency, as opposed to what AI production conveys. They will create entourages of artists, which will only add to the brand world through their own personalities. In a culture fed by rapid AI production, it is only slowness and realness that makes value tangible. Unprecedented velocity results in haste. What we crave the most is to define ourselves with trust and value. Which is how handmade dominates the visual language of today.

items.title: I want to bottle up places from my childhood.
items.subtitle: I have an undeniable urge to be able to preserve spaces.
items.excerpt: Everyone takes photos, all the time. I do, too. In fact, I have images sitting in my photos app more than anyone I know. I take photos to remember. My efforts certainly are not to catch a high aesthetic, of me or of anything else. I just tap. It is me, my point of view, I would…
items.html:
Everyone takes photos, all the time. I do, too. In fact, I have images sitting in my photos app more than anyone I know. I take photos to remember. My efforts certainly are not to catch a high aesthetic, of me or of anything else. I just tap. It is me, my point of view, I would like to freeze in time. And just in time, I discovered something more captivating than a snapshot. 3D scanning is not new tech. It has been around for quite some time. I just happened to get quite weirdly emotional with it. I am captivated by its meaning.

Gaussian splatting is done in seconds now. It is fairly easy to view a splat on a VR headset. I am sure there are many ways of going about it. It is the 360 degree view of a place, seen in first person point of view. The first time I experienced it, I cried. I took a 3D scan of my grandmother’s house before leaving Istanbul. It was my last refuge to bottle it up. She would be moving out of the place after my departure, the very place I visited every week when I was a kid. Countless times I have stayed over, made pillow forts, left my toothbrush there. I was no visitor. Because my parents became parents quite young, I was a regular in that house. After a couple months in Toronto, I decided to use that 3D scan as a material for a project. I was doing Digital Futures MDes at OCAD, during which we dealt with interactive technologies a lot. I put on my Meta VR headset. I turned my head around. There I was, sitting on the floor of the living room. The heirloom kilim on the floor beneath me, its motifs very visible.

Subscribe now

What this is, is freezing a moment in time and space. Being able to freeze the withering forces affecting objects, of three-dimensionality. Things are lost. They are destroyed. Nothing stays in their existing condition, ever. There is both a beauty to mortality, and agony. Being able to deceive it, however, is poetic. I will never touch it again. My hand will never travel on that kilim that covered the floor I grew up in. But I will forever have access to the scene. I will continue to see it as it was. Seeing as a sensory stimulus is perhaps the trigger of the decade. Constant sight and bottomless scrolling feeds our needs and wants. We see, want, react.

I experienced a simulation of the feelings I felt when I was casually hanging out with the warmth of my grandma. I have relived a deep personal history. I am still a little kid unaware. There is TV blasting news full volume. Certain scents coming from the kitchen and my grandpa, who I never met, staring from inside a fifty-year-old photo frame. After such an intense experience, one feels displaced. Right after I took off the headset, I was back in my Toronto condo. The colour hues differ so harshly. In an instant, yellows and oranges are washed away by cold blues. Where was I? What year was this I was living in? Where is my grandma? It is a slap in the face. I remember a moment I haven’t remembered in a long time. A seemingly unimportant moment came vivid and swift to me on a cold December evening. Thousands of kilometres away from the physical location. A brief expectancy of her walking in left me with a sizzling nausea from inertia of the headset.

A personal archive came alive but at the same time became equally impossible to hold. Having it stored on a cloud, on an invisible line of code, adds a layer of meaning I am not yet ready to embrace. Somewhere inaccessible on the earth stores my grandma’s home. If all came crushing down, where would I rush to save it? Am I understanding the working principles of it correctly? Perhaps not. Technicality is of no use, but the human experience is. Trails of real places, on a cloud existing in code, processed by a silicon intelligence. Something once so physical, is now not so much. Once, I accessed it every single week by foot. We lived pretty close to this house. It was the simplest thing, it had a door.

“Somewhere inaccessible on the earth stores my grandma’s home. If all came crushing down, where would I rush to save it?… Trails of real places, on a cloud existing in code, processed by a silicon intelligence. Something once so physical, is now not so much.”

Just like everyone else, I am searching my niche as a creative. As I progress in my weekly writings, I uncover so much about me to me. Holding on and recreating past experiences in forms of creative simulations has become an interest of mine without me realizing. Although it might sound like a negative muscle, holding on doesn’t have to mean to create a conservative commentary of the world. It is not resisting growth or positive change. To hold on to oneself might mean recreating oneself based on real experiences of the past. To be able to create based on past sights, patterns, objects and rituals. To ones like me with such fragile and limited memories, the ability to conserve carries so much weight. I really do love 3D scanning. I love to cry because of it. I would choose a cry for a place existing no more over any uninteresting emotional stimulus, ever.

items.title: I want to hold tech in my hands.
items.subtitle: The allure of using simple tech as a refuge, a drop of nostalgia and a flex.
items.excerpt: I’m writing this week’s luck bug post in the neighbourhood I was born in. As someone intoxicated with personal histories, it gives me an immense joy to circle back around on the Earth to find the pin on the map where I started. A spiritual checkpoint makes me think about me as a…
items.html:
I’m writing this week’s luck bug post in the neighbourhood I was born in. As someone intoxicated with personal histories, it gives me an immense joy to circle back around on the Earth to find the pin on the map where I started. A spiritual checkpoint makes me think about me as a child and my early passions. I loved tech as I still do today.

I was the Nintendo kid, but I also had a PSP, a Wii, an iPod and, of course, the first ever iPad. I had a DVD player for when travelling and a CD player passed down from my mom. I made playlists and burned them on CDs. I named them using permanent markers. I displayed my Sims CDs in my room on a shelf.

I no longer own any tech device that can run a CD. My TV doesn’t have the red-yellow-white cable inputs the Wii connects to. The batteries on my iPods are cooked. iPad, I am sure, ended up in a landfill. Yet, I am still actively searching Ebay for a modded iPod and I collect Youtube videos of past games I played online. I have an unwavering motivation to keep accessing these older hardware and software. I love the nostalgia. But more than that, I love to simulate the past experience of technology. Specifically having one function for a single device, and the luxury of concentrating yourself to that single function when using it.

The intimidation I experience with the current course of AI developments makes me run away to dumber tech. Regardless of the symbiotic relationship I formed with AI and Apple and everything new, fast and metaverse; I still find simple tech cool. And I am not alone.

Subscribe now

Simple tech is cool because it is a distant memory. Using simple tech is a reenactment of simpler times. The iPod is jewellery. The haptics on that white circle in the very middle is a motion my thumb will never forget. All muscle memory. You have to spend a ridiculous amount of time to unknot the wired ear buds. May it be a ritual. Showing cables tangled inside your hair, a statement. A statement to the world that says see, I am analogue like that. I still believe in romance. I am a romantic, I am real. I unknot. I chose inconvenience.

Why do we yearn for more tactility in the technological devices we use?

The touch screen has become almost like another limb. The glass surface is slippery, lacking any real friction between us and the digital world. Maybe we need more friction because the line between real and unreal has become a bit too blurry for us to survive. Maybe this is what that is, a survival instinct. The performances we put up for what’s behind the black slippery glass has made us obsessive and depressed beings with attention spans of several seconds. We have forgotten that what matters is here and now. Hence, we started wanting less.

“ The glass surface is slippery, lacking any real friction between us and the digital world. Maybe we need more friction because the line between real and unreal has become a bit too blurry for us to survive. Maybe this is what that is, a survival instinct.”

Visuals make the world. A girl reading from an old pink Nintendo DS makes her hard to attain. Adds a layer to her mystique. She is even using the small pen to scroll down. Highlights a text. Slaps it close and puts it in her pocket. A private possession she owns, inaccessible by the internet. With tactility and simpleness comes a detachment from the web that surrounds everything we do. Privacy for something we would not demand privacy for. It wouldn’t cross our minds that someone might want our reading data. But we know even that data could be stolen, because it has already been sold between tech oligarchs twice by today.

Yearning to hold is not new. What is new is the context.

items.title: I bought a keychain from Toronto’s Pearson Airport
items.subtitle: On creating a sense of belonging to a life built elsewhere. & collecting seemingly non-functional physical objects for “Reverse Memory Anchoring”.
items.excerpt: I took the plane from Toronto Pearson airport to Istanbul three weeks ago. Unaware if and when I would be returning, I found the souvenir store nearest to my gate. My hand immediately reached for the keychains. Most of them, I presume, were left unsold from the early 2000s. The…
items.html:
I took the plane from Toronto Pearson airport to Istanbul three weeks ago. Unaware if and when I would be returning, I found the souvenir store nearest to my gate. My hand immediately reached for the keychains. Most of them, I presume, were left unsold from the early 2000s. The aesthetic and colour choices were still intact. Some were bejewelled, some were wooden. Almost all either had a Canadian flag or a CN Tower on it. I couldn’t let them go, although I practically had no use for the object. I held each option one by one in my palm, imagining myself doing the same thing once I was back in Istanbul. A subtle squeeze to the Canada keychain would be the perfect ritual to remind me here, this moment. And I needed a reminder. So I kept on squeezing each keychain until I landed on one with the Canadian flag. I hung it on my backpack. A new function had appeared for an object long forgotten in an airport souvenir corner: replenishing my belief in the life I would like to create. A physical object to visualize the possibility of a life elsewhere.

“This is a complete inversion of that. A souvenir for a moment not yet lived. An intent planted for the future. Reverse memory anchoring.”

The souvenir has a presumed functionality. The root location is set from the moment of manufacture. They are bought and then showcased around home as reminders of the good times spent in foreign lands. This is a complete inversion of that. A souvenir for a moment not yet lived. An intent planted for the future. Reverse memory anchoring. More so a collectible to anchor those intentions on. A collectible is an empty canvas you fill with meaning. The keychain here was a vessel to connect me to Toronto, which I treated as a collectible rather than a souvenir. My behaviour resembled that of a collector. Because my motivation was not only to remember a time elsewhere, it was to precisely remember the idea behind it. The keychain helped me visualize myself hopping on that return plane to Toronto.

Subscribe now

My dilemma was ignited by my status as a ghost in Toronto, never receiving any replies to my cold emails whatsoever; meanwhile my mom was having casual day drinks with her social circle in Istanbul which features business owners and director-level white collars. It is true that melting pots melt your existing network as well. If no one answers my calls in Toronto, I might have to return home to Istanbul to call others, to make me happen. I have no real standing offer at the moment, but I know I’d at least be seen. Which forced me to make this purchase of a small but hopeful gesture, a small squeeze. A final push.

What I needed was a small door in time to travel through. A physical proof of existence. When feeling lost becomes a motive stretched in time, refuge to the easiest option out of many seems logical. Easy, meaning a life in Istanbul. The keychain was also a proof that returning might not be as easy as it sounds. Embracing the duty of making things work out elsewhere requires gut and insistence. Considering that spending a little more than a week at my parents’ house means the conversations about what I’ll do with my life start up again, I knew I needed it to tie me to that specific moment at the gate. I felt content with Toronto. So much so that I needed a piece of it with me.

Collectibles are tiny plastic Sony Angels with bare bums that live on our bathroom shelves. What is significant about people who buy non-functional items, like me, is that we tie a specific, private, ungraspable meaning to these objects. For example almost every single time I’m on my way back to Toronto, I drop a Littlest Pet Shop toy (small animal toys with bubble heads) from my childhood into one of my bags. One time even mom brought one as I was walking out of my childhood home, unasked. The meaning I tie is inexplicable and complex. Even for me, the one constructing the superstition. Perhaps it’s the ability to carry a part of my childhood with me. To a land I have no history in. When the mind seeks to rationalize but fails to do so, it finds physical objects to be highly comforting and useful.

Maybe it is that permission to not rationalize and understand that makes this possession valuable. The object itself is where you put a feeling you can’t yet explain. You don’t have to explain the feeling to keep it.

items.title: A Mediterranean summer can be exercised anywhere.
items.subtitle: An exercise for the city this summer.
items.excerpt: White-walled cottages line hills on rocky terrain. €10 is a decent price for a plate of fried calamari. Days are long and in technicolor. Yes, friend. You are probably somewhere in the Mediterranean. Anywhere . Everywhere. The emphasis there is intentional. Even in a sea of…
items.html:
White-walled cottages line hills on rocky terrain. €10 is a decent price for a plate of fried calamari. Days are long and in technicolor. Yes, friend. You are probably somewhere in the Mediterranean.

Anywhere. Everywhere. The emphasis there is intentional. Even in a sea of concrete walls and hills of shimmering condo windows, it is possible to practice a daily flow grounded in our own nature. Our responsibilities might keep us in the city, unable to hop on the euro summer train. Time might feel stretched out, because we would rather be somewhere near the sea. In especially these times that we need to be reminded: anywhere can be a launching pad for a summer lived intentionally.

This is not a piece of writing that glamorizes any new-age self-help phenomenon. Yes, eventually it will tell you to go outside and to live in the moment. But I promise it doesn’t repeat what is already said a thousand times over. The idea to this article formed out of my pure joy to be in Toronto this summer. As unhinged as it may sound, yes, a summer spent in Toronto has triggered this article. I spent quite literally months near the Aegean Sea, because my parents own a summer house in Bodrum. It is a special place. My brain overloads with ideas. This happens to be one of them, so bear with me.

luck bug is where I chase the ideas that overload my brain. one essay a week, free. subscribe and let a little luck find you.

Share

Thyself on vacation

It’s no secret that a limited time outside our normal does wonders to our understanding of the world around us. Suddenly we are thrown into a simulation of foreign visions and customs. We learn to adapt by being exposed to the alien, in return we learn so much about ourselves. About what’s possible in life, and us in those new situations. The Mediterranean premise is very similar to that feeling of awe we might feel when we come face to face with something so other, to the point where we might not care about who we are anymore. We purely indulge in the moment.

The Mediterranean suddenly seems so other because of its construction of freedom. The physical setting, the nonchalant culture and slower daily pace reassures this is the experience you get when you’re there. There are coves that are only accessible by trails. Water so virgin, there is no boat in sight. The very fact that the islands are isolated from any mainland makes them feel a lot like a blind spot. There are no roads that lead anywhere. There are no invisible social rules. No one will give you the slightest side eye. This is the place that has invented the laidback life. Self consciousness doesn’t survive under the midday sun. Turquoise blue hypnotizes the eyes. Your attention is only reserved for the views. The pace of living, too, is much slower. There is no timetable, and the day starts and ends in its own pace. You are freed from acting as an entity all the time. The individual self relaxes in its human costume.

Philosophies from the sea

Centuries ago, the same soil and water has bred the ancient philosophers. What’s significant is how these philosophers of the ancient world reached meaning. They reached conclusions about life through examining outside world and the changes in nature. Thales thought everything was made up of water. The gaze was directed outside. Heraclitus watched a river and came up with the idea that everything was in constant change in the world. He was the one then, who arrived at conclusions about the inside through examining outside. He said: I searched out myself. Through understanding the world around him, he understood himself. To look in, was to look out. Finding yourself and forgetting yourself was the same practice.

When I look into the hyper-individualized world of the west today, suggesting to forget oneself sounds like the totally opposite of what people might recognize as remedy. Because the self-help genre has been obsessed about defining oneself in order to find it. However, chasing self-definition is its own trap. Definition seeking mindset creates a loop, stuck with thinking about what you are, over and over again. The escape is to not think about definition, but focus on the living part.

As Žižek paraphrases Lacan: “the obsession to know oneself is in itself a pathology... You are not cured when you are satisfied…but when you simply don’t matter to yourself…” This is certainly not an article to bring in a full fashioned philosophical argument (especially with Žižek involved). What the Mediterranean premise is, is the opposite of the western self-obsession. Ancient and modern, the same outward facing culture is continuous. Turning the gaze outward, even for a specific amount of time, will prove useful to reduce the pressures there are to constantly reinvent and define what’s inside.

Leave a comment

Tips for experimentation this summer

Note that the summer hasn’t ended yet, no matter what the public opinion is. Embrace and elongate your hard earned summer.

Building on top of the picture I painted above, I would like to create an exercise. Summertime is perfect for a personal breakthrough. Spring is when the hardships of winter melt away, and fall marks the start of a new year. Summertime belongs to ourselves, even though it means remaining in the city. Metaphorically, our bodies wake up from a winter long freeze to enjoy the heat of the day. With movement comes wisdom. Summer is for taking action.

Play with the rhythm of your day

Rhythm is the experience of time. It is the difference in activities that feel longer or shorter in time. The frustration of time not flowing as fast while holding a plank, or that surprisingly fast first hour of meeting a close friend. Rhythm is also how much action our bodies bear while doing something. The BPM of the song on the dance floor, or cold plunging. One of the main pillars of shifting your attention from inside to outside of the body is to play with the rhythm of our bodies.

Our bodies being our sensory system to communicate with the outer world, the body is the first thing to experiment with. When in somewhere else, rhythm changes because of the change in activities. Location change is a powerful flux for the body. In the city, when nothing else changed in your daily flow, you might have experienced this when a friend comes visiting as a tourist. As if looking at the same surroundings from a different set of eyes, hosting someone changes your regular week. A rhythm shift happens. Move your body in unconventional ways. Prioritize physical actions. Activate your sensory system.

Adjust your daily schedule. It could be staying in bed late on a Sunday. It could also be finding somewhere to move or to stay still. Shock your internal expectations for a day. Play with the experience of bodily sensations. If you have been taking refuge in doomscrolling, experiment with screen free time. Let time stretch. Or let it slip away. When making plans, consider the patterns of your day.

Be flexible with your choices

Flexibility is allowing opportunities to arise on its own. It is the spontaneity, the lack of timetable in the equation. It is that laidback life that we are exposed to in the Mediterranean, reenacted. Resist the need to meticulously plan your days. Accept the changes in course and cherish them. Being flexible in choices requires a little bit of internal reassurance. Be content with your choice even if the outcome could be mediocre.

Note that allowing new things should not always mean a new way to spend your hard earned money. It may also mean walking ten blocks on a random afternoon, or talking with someone you have been avoiding for some time. Allowing impulsive wants will need practice. Given the effort, flexibility will reward you with unexpected opportunities. Without walking those ten blocks, you cannot know the kinds of ideas that might cross your mind walking. Some things only find us when we allow unexpected to happen.

Express your contentedness

Being vocal about things you find beautiful around you is how you internalize your happiness. You may sound cheesy, but so be it. Clearly voice why and how you like what’s around you. Allow your inner peace to be expressed. Expression will automatically result in turning your gaze outside rather than in. It is our ability to make our contentedness concrete by expression. Personally, I love to gaze to a moving body of water. Maybe it’s from my days of watching the Bosphorus strait in Istanbul. Wherever I am on the Earth, I like to see some water. I always express my pleasure in doing so.

To have the actual content to talk about, always prefer a plan outside over inside. Always make time to walk somewhere, or bike! This is THE season for city bikes. When in parks, view what’s around you with curiosity. Take advantage of the scenery. Acknowledge the differences of the city streets in summer compared to winter. Take the risk of being that boring friend. Hear yourself saying it out loud.

Verdict

The idea behind this article is to inspire you into breaking certain habits you might form along the year. A trip to Icarus might be the answer to your woes, but exercising a similar mindset might give you the joy you never knew you needed. I have never been a type A person, and I certainly don’t define myself as a type B. I don’t believe in types. I only believe in shock therapies. And I love to break some rules. Break some rules yourself. Enjoy the sun while we still can in the northern hemisphere and talk about it to other people. Embrace playfulness, and travel to the Mediterranean whenever you can.

The photos are shot by myself in Bodrum & Mykonos. Bodrum has shaped my whole first hand experience of a Mediterranean living. I arrived for my yearly holiday here two days ago after a 16-hour long journey from Toronto. I designed the card as a 3D archive of my own of my experience of the Mediterranean summer.
